STATES.name: Andhra Pradesh

confirms: 7-working-day statutory timeline confirmed with a precise citation: Rule 3 of the AP Factories Rules, 1950, as amended by G.O.Ms.No.7/2022 (2 Mar 2022), which cut the window from 30 days to 7 days and moved filing online via the Single Desk Portal.
>20-worker threshold independently confirmed: AP's own amendment to Sec 2(m)/85(1) sets 20 workers with power (matches the ED) / 40 workers without power.
newDetail: AP has a state-wide statutory deemed-approval framework for industrial clearances generally (AP Industrial Single Window Clearance Act, 2002), and green/white category industries get deemed approval to commence within 3 years of a self-declared undertaking under the Industrial Policy 2020-23 — this nuances the ED's "no deemed approval actively invoked" into "exists in law, rarely invoked in practice" rather than contradicting it.
Two further 2025 Factories Rules amendments (G.O.Ms.No.19, G.O.Ms.No.22) and a draft Safety Audit Rules 2025 were found but their content could not be confirmed online.
sources: G.O.Ms.No.7/2022, AP Factories (Amendment) Rules 2022
AP Sec 2(m)/85(1) worker-threshold amendment
AP Industrial Single Window Clearance Act, 2002
secondary.notes: Confirms the 7-day statutory timeline with an exact citation (Rule 3, as amended by G.O.Ms.No.7/2022) and the >20-worker threshold. Adds nuance rather than contradiction on deemed approval: a state-wide statutory deemed-approval framework exists for industrial clearances generally, which fits "exists in law, not actively invoked" rather than "absent." Current fee-schedule figures could not be verified online (only a clearly outdated 1994 reference was found).

Risk threshold: more than 20 workers requires a license; fewer than 20 is generally exempt, except specified hazardous categories under Section 85(1) (rice/dal mills, saw mills, small engineering works, etc.) which require a license even with fewer than 10 workers.
Best practice: inspection findings are published via the Central Inspection System (CIS) portal.

fgd.meta: 12 participants, Manufacturing (mixed), APIIC One Stop Service Centre, Atchuthapuram, Anakapalli · 29 Sept 2026 · 47 min
fgd.process: Filed online on the AP Single Window Portal. Scrutiny queries are raised on the portal and by phone, and mostly handled by the consultant rather than the applicant. Inspection occurs roughly one week after submission on average, followed by further scrutiny and final approval. Applicants cannot see this internal sequence — the portal shows only "pending" or "pending upload," with the first visible sign of approval being the printed certificate itself. The electrical department sits entirely outside the single-window portal.
fgd.timeline: Most participants reported no delay in scrutiny or inspection itself, but significant time is lost before submission preparing the stability study and drawings. One participant recalled a case of roughly 6 months' delay (details unclear).
fgd.automation: "We have filed everything on the single window portal, but we still have to knock on every door." The portal's 20MB upload limit is too small for a full drawing set (some industries need 50-100MB). No real-time or stage-wise tracking exists.
fgd.documentsNote: No duplicate/redundant documents reported; drawings uploaded once are retained on the portal and carried forward at the annual acknowledgment stage unless the structure is modified.
fgd.deemed: Not described as an operative mechanism — the only visible signal of status is the final printed certificate.
costs: Substantive
Building stability study obtained at the applicant's own cost from a government-empaneled structural/civil engineer; fee varies by engineer and industry size.
Intermediary
Consultants used end-to-end, described as near-essential for small industries lacking in-house technical knowledge (AutoCAD drawings "effectively essential"). Not quantified in INR.
Statutory
Fee calculated online on horsepower/kVA, labour and workforce, paid directly to government. Participants explicitly did not ask for fee reduction.
Informal / unrecorded
"No unrecorded or informal costs were reported; every cost in the process can be recorded in the books" — a notably clean finding relative to other States.
complaints: Introduce real-time, stage-wise application tracking with timelines, modeled on the AP incentive portal — called the single most important ask.
Raise the 20MB upload limit to 50-100MB.
Publish an FAQ/guidance document listing mandatory documents and technical specifications by industry category, plus safety guidelines.
Invest in skill development/skill mapping — framed as preferable to fee reduction.
contradictions: The official single-window framing is contradicted: the electrical department sits entirely outside the portal, so applicants must separately approach it — "we still have to knock on every door."

No deemed-approval mechanism is visible in practice; despite the 7-working-day statutory timeline, applicants get no interim status and learn of approval only when the certificate prints — participants called this an "Implementation Gap."

STATES.name: Chhattisgarh

contradicts: The Chhattisgarh Ease of Doing Business Bill, 2026 was passed by the Legislative Assembly on 16 July 2026 — reported as a risk-based, trust-based permission framework with deemed/auto-approval after 30-60 days (by category) and self-certification for low-risk units, across an initial 43 services. If Factory License is among those services and the Bill is now in force, this would directly contradict the ED's "no deemed approval mechanism identified" — but Governor's assent, gazette notification, commencement date, and whether Factory License is covered could not be confirmed as of this research.
newDetail: A low-confidence secondary source suggests a possible Rule 5 validity change from 10 to 15 years (notification RULE-5/39/2025-LABOUR, Aug 2025) — unconfirmed against primary text, but worth chasing since the ED gave no validity figure at all for Chhattisgarh.
Chhattisgarh's Single Window System 2.0 / "OneClick" portal relaunched in July 2024 — single login, e-challan payment, department queries routed through the portal.
sources: Chhattisgarh Ease of Doing Business Bill 2026 — press coverage (Drishti IAS, PTI, Deccan Chronicle, Jul 2026)
Chhattisgarh Single Window System 2.0 relaunch coverage (Jul 2024)
secondary.notes: The dominant finding is forward-looking: a new state law (Assembly-passed 16 Jul 2026) would introduce exactly the deemed-approval mechanism the ED said does not exist — but whether it has commenced, and whether Factory License is among its covered services, could not be confirmed. Treat the ED's "no deemed approval" as likely accurate at interview time, but possibly going stale within months. The FGD's "30-day prescribed timeline" and the official fee schedule could not be independently verified from any other official source.

fgd.meta: 5 participants (the source document labels them "Experts," though this is a business/user FGD), Directorate of Industries, Commerce & Industry, Raipur · 7 Aug 2026 · 1hr14min
fgd.process: Factory Licence is understood as the final stage, gated by prior approvals (land, building plan, fire, electricity, pollution) — delays upstream cascade into Factory Licence delay. Online filing itself is "not considered difficult"; the bottleneck is internal departmental movement and follow-up. A portal migration caused previously submitted documents to become unavailable, forcing fresh uploads.
fgd.timeline: A 30-day prescribed timeline was referenced, but actual time is driven by inter-departmental movement, described as "a significant source of delay." No specific real-world day count was given.
fgd.automation: "The biggest issue is that the single-window portal exists, but the departments are not fully interconnected." There is no clear online status showing exactly where, or at which department, an application is stuck.
fgd.documentsNote: The same government information is requested at multiple approval stages (duplication across departments); documents submitted under the old portal were lost in the migration and had to be re-uploaded.
fgd.deemed: Not described as operative; the emphasis is entirely on the lack of visibility into where an application is stuck, not on any automatic-grant mechanism.
costs: Intermediary
A consultant is hired specifically to track applications and resolve pending issues, since applicants do not always know where an application is pending or what is needed next. Not quantified in INR.
complaints: Designate one nodal department to coordinate and track all factory-related approvals.
Auto-reuse previously submitted documents/information — a "DigiLocker-type repository" was explicitly suggested.
Provide clear, stage-wise online status: what is pending, at which department.
Run land, building-plan, fire, electricity, pollution and Factory Licence approvals in parallel.
Provide checklists, sample documents and step-by-step guidance to reduce avoidable consultant dependence.
contradictions: A direct, explicit contradiction of any "integrated single window" framing: "the single-window portal exists, but the departments are not fully interconnected" — participants explicitly called for a move from a "single portal" approach to a genuinely "single process" approach.

STATES.name: Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu

newDetail: A draft DNH & DD Ease of Doing Business Regulation, 2026 (gazetted 20 Jul 2026 for consultation) proposes a "Right to Business" self-declaration / in-principle-approval framework for eligible MSMEs — conceptually adjacent to, but distinct from, a classic "25 days then deemed granted" timer. It suggests practice may be running ahead of, or anticipating, formal rule change, which is a plausible explanation for why the FGD reports a working 25-day deemed-approval rule that the ED does not confirm.

Possible legal fragmentation: a 2026 draft OSH rules document references the "Goa, Daman & Diu Factories Rules, 1985" as still applicable specifically to Daman — the Daman side of the merged UT may still run under older pre-merger rules distinct from a single unified "DNH&DD Factories Rules," which could itself explain reporting variance.
sources: DNH&DD draft Ease of Doing Business Regulation 2026 (Official Gazette, 20 Jul 2026)
Adapted Gujarat (Right of Citizens to Public Services) Act, 2013, as applied to the UT
secondary.notes: Could not resolve the central ED-vs-FGD discrepancy (whether a 25-day deemed-approval rule formally exists) from any official rule text found online. The most likely statutory home identified is the UT's adapted Right of Citizens to Public Services Act, which typically carries per-service time limits with deemed-grant provisions, but its schedule of services could not be retrieved to confirm. A draft 2026 "Right to Business" regulation suggests the UT is actively moving toward the kind of fast-track regime the FGD already describes experiencing.

Ownership/lease deed, list of directors, safety clearances (for licence registration)

deemedApproval.text: None currently — approval is granted only after actual scrutiny and site inspection by the safety officer. The expert suggested exploring a deemed-approval clause for cases where scrutiny is not completed within a defined period, without diluting site inspection for high-risk units.

remarks: No risk-based classification system currently exists — all applications go through the same scrutiny and mandatory inspection regardless of scale or risk.

No duplicate/redundant documentation flagged; the checklist is deliberately kept concise at 7 documents. Main friction: some documents still have to be submitted offline despite an otherwise online process.
DNH & DD has one of the highest concentrations of industrial units among UTs (~7,000 registered industries).
An amendment provision (e.g. change in occupier/premises) is currently missing online — not carried over from the earlier manual process.
Monthly departmental review meetings on portal performance; sector-specific awareness seminars.
Portal is linked with the National Single Window portal for cross-visibility.
dataGaps: Exact validity slabs and fee schedule not confirmed during the discussion

fgd.meta: 6 participants, Mixed sector, Vidhyut Bhavan, Daman · 5 Aug 2026 · 53 min 47 sec
fgd.process: Almost entirely online. The department publishes a clear checklist; once documents are ready, completing and submitting the form takes 30-45 minutes. Physical inspection is NOT required for standard, self-declaration-based (Green category) licensing — applicants self-certify products, machinery, electrical load, workforce and floor area. Inspection IS required for higher-risk (Orange/Red) categories. Factory Licensing, Pollution Control Clearance, Town Planning and Power are all accessible via the National Single Window Portal.
fgd.timeline: Deemed approval kicks in at 25 days if the department neither raises a query nor acts. Orange/Red (inspection-required) cases take up to ~25 days due to site-visit scheduling. When a query is raised, "the clock pauses until the applicant responds," then resumes promptly — described as functioning largely as intended.
fgd.automation: Largely positive — officers and the portal are described as "responsive and supportive," communicating via SMS, email and a dedicated departmental WhatsApp group. The one friction point: local telecom/internet infrastructure in industrial belts can stall online submissions, particularly during heavy monsoons.
fgd.documentsNote: No redundant or duplicate documentation reported. The checklist (building layout drawings, land ownership/title records, rent/purchase agreement, fire department permission) is described as "clear and non-repetitive."
fgd.deemed: The one State in this pilot where deemed approval is reported as actually working — the 25-day rule, paused only by genuine queries and resuming promptly, with no reports of businesses having to chase the department.
costs: Intermediary
Consultant fee for layout drawings/technical paperwork ≈ ₹30,000 for smaller enterprises specifically to avoid errors and repeated queries — "the fee is high for the service."
Substantive
Machinery/equipment must be purchased or upgraded to meet license-mandated specifications, a cost separate from and additional to normal capacity-building spend.
Delay / financing

Where a business depends on bank loans or government tender-based supply contracts, delay in the licence and pollution clearance directly delays loan disbursement/billing, adding an interest-cost burden while waiting.
Statutory
Example fee ≈ ₹22,000, calculated automatically by the portal from connected load, workforce and pollution category. Participants explicitly said no hidden charges were reported.
complaints: Adopt a graduated/tiered compliance timeline for newer, lower-risk units — explicitly citing Gujarat's practice of giving green/low-risk units up to 2-3 years to complete peripheral compliances after starting operations, as a model DNH/DD currently lacks.
Strengthen telecom/internet infrastructure in industrial belts to prevent monsoon-related submission outages.

Formally empanel/register consultants for factory licensing (currently unregistered) — contrasted with architects on the OBPS portal and certified water-compliance auditors, who must hold recognised credentials.
contradictions: Largely CONFIRMS rather than contradicts the official narrative — deemed approval, portal responsiveness and fee transparency are all corroborated by businesses.

The main nuance: the official narrative's statutory fee (~₹22,000) understates the true cost of compliance — the FGD surfaces real but unquantified substantive (equipment) and delay/financing costs that sit outside the official fee schedule.

STATES.name: Himachal Pradesh

contradicts: The official OFRIS portal FAQ states "Approval of Plans — 3 months" and "Registration & Renewal of factory licence — 30 days" — a 90-day/30-day pairing, not the ED's 30-day/45-day pairing. Could not confirm which figure is current; flagged as an open discrepancy rather than resolved either way.

HP's Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions (HP) Rules — the "OSH Code framework" the ED cited — are still in DRAFT form (~22 May 2026 version, 45-day objection window), not yet in force. Licensing today still operates under the Factories Act 1948 / HP Factories Rules 1950 (as amended 2023-2025), so the ED's framing may describe an anticipated reform track rather than the rules actually governing licensing right now.
newDetail: Two recent amendments confirmed: HP Factories (Amendment) Rules 2024 (30 Aug 2024) replaced the one-year licence fee schedule and added a Chief-Inspector-recognised "competent person" provision for tests/inspections; HP Factories (Amendment) Rules 2025 (16 Oct 2025) revised working-hour provisions.

The 2024 amendment's own title ("fee for grant of licence for one year") suggests fees may scale with the chosen validity period, nuancing the ED's "fees independent of validity" claim — not confirmed either way.
sources: OFRIS portal guidelines & FAQ (ofris.hp.gov.in)
HP Factories (Amendment) Rules 2024 & 2025
Draft HP Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Rules, 2026
secondary.notes: The official OFRIS portal FAQ gives a different day-count pairing (90/30) than the ED's (30/45), and the ED's framing of an "OSH Code framework" appears to describe a still-draft reform rather than the rules currently in force. Two 2024-2025 amendments were confirmed with citations. The deemed-approval provision and Fire/Pollution NOC exemption claims could not be independently verified.

No major burdensome activity identified; the key pending reform is full Single Window System integration — the portal is already structurally aligned with it, but direct submission via the Single Window is not yet enabled.

STATES.name: Jammu & Kashmir

confirms: The 30-day timeline is confirmed via two independent legal bases: a June 2018 amendment to the J&K Factories Rules (licence granted within 30 days of application, consistent with the ED's "clock pauses on query" description) and SRO-467 (Oct 2018), separately listing 30 days for the Factories Act registration certificate.

Risk-based colour classification confirmed with exact thresholds: Red (Pollution Index ≥60), Orange (41-59), Green (21-40), White (≤20) — and a 28 Feb 2025 order adopted the CPCB's Jan 2025 classification, exempting the White category entirely from Consent to Establish/Operate — a recent reform not in the ED summary.
contradicts: The ED cited "Public Services Guarantee Act, 2018" — every source instead names the parent statute the J&K Public Services Guarantee Act, 2011 (Act IX of 2011); "2018" appears to be the year of the specific SRO/Rules amendment that operationalised it for Factories, not the Act's own year.

On the penal provision being "monitored, not yet active": the PSGA's officer-penalty mechanism (fines deducted from the responsible officer's honorarium, compensation to the applicant) appears to be actively enforced elsewhere in J&K government — e.g. penalty proceedings reported against 55 Revenue Dept officers — suggesting the mechanism is live state-wide even if no specific instance was found for Factories Department delays.
newDetail: The official J&K Single Window portal hosts a genuine citizen-charter-grade document checklist for Factory Registration — 15 distinct items (4 mutually-exclusive tenure-proof alternatives), more granular than the ED's "12-13 documents" estimate: Form No.1 application; Form 2 & 3 combined (annual); Pollution Board Consent to Establish/Operate; NOC from a specified authority (only for sawmills, wood-peeling, explosives, arms & ammunition, drug/pharma factories, brick kilns, stone crushers); Manager's authorisation letter; Power Sanction Certificate copy; Safety Certificate (duplicate); Manager/Occupier photo; applicant ID proof; one of land records/rent deed/allotment letter/lease deed; DIC Registration approval copy; machinery list; process flow chart; project report; site plan (triplicate).
sources: J&K Single Window — official SOP & procedure checklist, service id 21 (singlewindow.jk.gov.in)
SRO-467, Oct 2018
J&K Pollution Control Committee classification order, 28 Feb 2025
secondary.notes: Confirms the 30-day timeline from two independent legal bases, and finds a genuinely more granular official 15-item document checklist than the ED's own "12-13 documents" estimate (transcribed in full below). One correction: the ED's "PSGA 2018" is actually the PSGA 2011, operationalised for Factories via a 2018 notification. The officer-penalty mechanism the ED called dormant appears to be actively enforced elsewhere in J&K government.

timeline.basis: Prescribed processing timeline under the Public Services Guarantee Act, 2018 — no deemed-approval/penal provision currently in force
timeline.text: 30 days; the clock stops when a query is pending with the applicant and restarts on resubmission. Delays are common where applicants or their service providers are slow to respond — sometimes 2-3 months pending at the applicant's end.

documents: Constitution documents (MOA/directors list/Board Resolution, or proprietorship/partnership declaration)
STATES.documentsNote: On average 12-13 documents, varying by size/category. No additional documents are required unless the activity is specialised (e.g. fertiliser manufacturing).

deemedApproval.text: None currently exists. A penal/automatic-approval provision under the Public Services Guarantee Act, 2018 is periodically monitored (reviewed by the Chief Secretary) but not yet in force. The expert suggested that low-risk, document-complete applications could move toward a deemed/same-day approval.

validity.text: Not separately addressed for the initial licence; discussed mainly for renewal (1-5 years, independent of risk category, at the applicant's choice).

fees.text: Not specified — no numerical fee structure given.

remarks: Risk-based colour classification (Red/Orange/White/Green) from the Pollution Control Board; Red = hazardous (e.g. pesticide manufacturing). Physical inspection is more likely for Red-category, but even White/Green units are inspected in ~90% of registration cases.

Key inefficiency: no inter-departmental document auto-verification (e.g. auto-fetch of Pollution Board/Fire NOC status) — applicants must separately upload documents already held by other departments on the same Single Window platform.
Governance issue: intermediaries/service providers file using their own mobile number/email rather than the applicant's, reducing accountability and traceability — "hijacked by the service provider."
Staff shortage relative to application volume causes delays; the Single Window platform has had periodic technical issues over the past year.
Common query cause: incorrect worker-count or power-load details in Form 23.
No clear amendment provision (change in occupier/premises) currently exists online. No QR-code-based certificate verification mechanism yet.

Quotes (Mohammad Youmis): "On average, a new factory licence requires twelve to thirteen documents..." · "Once a query is raised, the clock stops until the applicant resubmits; the thirty-day timeline resumes only after resubmission." · "This particular system has been hijacked by the service provider — the ID and phone number used are often the consultant's, not the applicant's." · "If the applicant simply has to give one declaration, the department should be able to process it directly, almost like a same-day approval."

STATES.name: Jharkhand

confirms: Issuing-authority hierarchy (Inspector → Deputy Chief Inspector → Chief Inspector) confirmed via a sample issued licence citing Section 6(1) of the Factories Act.

The 28 March 2025 Schedule A/B/C fee notification is confirmed to exist and fully replace the prior schedules, plus a flat ₹1,000 fee for both amendment and transfer — matching the ED's cited notification, though the exact per-slab rupee figures could not be independently re-verified.
newDetail: Licence validity is more precisely Rule 5(2): minimum 1 year up to a maximum of 15 years — more specific than the ED's vague "longer-term options."

The Jharkhand Single Window Clearance Act, 2016 already includes "Deemed Approval, Self-certification, Third-party inspections and Appeals" as general features of the state's single-window regime — a deemed-approval hook already exists in law; whether Factory License specifically is a scheduled service under it could not be confirmed, so the ED's "not yet implemented" claim is plausible, not disproven.
A new appeal mechanism (occupier may appeal a Chief Inspector order to the Secretary/Principal Secretary within 30 days) was found as a 2025 procedural addition not in the ED summary.
sources: Jharkhand Factories Amendment Rules 2025 notification, 28 Mar 2025

remarks: Significant compliance burden: repeated submission/manual verification of information already held by other government departments (land ownership, project details, environmental clearances) — the Single Window reduced physical interactions, but cross-departmental document verification remains a challenge.
Risk-based inspection framework: Low-Risk (streamlined route + inspection exemptions), Medium-Risk (third-party certification + joint verification), High-Risk (mandatory technical/site inspections).

Recommended reforms: a Master Factory Profile to reuse verified data; a consolidated deficiency memo (replacing repeated deficiency cycles); fully automated digital inspection management; system-to-system inter-departmental verification; streamlined/pre-filled licensing amendments.
Best practice: Shramadhan is a unified digital platform covering the full lifecycle — registration, licensing, renewal, amendment, inspection, fee, status.

STATES.name: Uttar Pradesh

confirms: Deemed approval is confirmed with statutory citation: the UP Factories (73rd Amendment) Rules, 2018 substituted Rule 3 so that plans/licences not rejected within the time limit are deemed approved, with licences for already-approved plans issued the same day. The exact trigger-day count embedded in the sub-rule could not be retrieved, but the mechanism itself is confirmed, consistent with the ED.

Validity of up to 10 years is confirmed under Rule 9 (2018 amendment) — with an added nuance the ED didn't mention: hazardous factories under Sec 2(cb) are capped at 5 years, and those also under the MSIHC Rules 1989 (the same hazardous carve-out the ED cites for the 30-day timeline) are capped at just 3 years.
contradicts: The official Nivesh Mitra portal's own service list states the Factory License timeline as 30 days (renewal separately at 60 days) — not the ED's 15 working days. newDetail: Nivesh Mitra 3.0 is confirmed as a real, recent consolidation (500+ services down to ~200-225, plus an AI chatbot/automated grievance handling) via official Invest UP press releases (Mar & Aug 2025) — but no independent, non-government coverage of user complaints was found, so the FGD's "confusing regression" complaint could be neither corroborated nor refuted from official sources.

A secondary compliance source separately noted physical inspection "remains mandatory" in UP's process — partially supports the FGD's contradiction of the ED's "no physical department visit required" claim, though this concerns the statutory site inspection rather than an office-filing visit specifically.

STATES.name: West Bengal

confirms: SilpaSathi's own official user manual states a 65-day WBRTPS timeline for a fresh licence — directly confirms the official's own "~65 days" figure with a citable source, rather than just his self-characterisation of it as "lengthy."
newDetail: The portal name, missing from the ED, is confirmed as SilpaSathi (silpasathi.wb.gov.in) — made the exclusive mandatory channel for Factory License from 1 January 2023 by a December 2022 Labour Dept notification, replacing the department's earlier standalone system.

No deemed-approval-to-applicant clause was found anywhere in the WB Right to Public Services Act framework — only a penalty on the delaying officer (₹250-1,000 fine), with no automatic grant to the applicant. This independently confirms the FGD's account (a real 3-4 month wait, no deemed-approval mechanism ever mentioned by business participants) over any assumption that West Bengal has an unstated safeguard.

Fees are set under Schedules A, B, C of the West Bengal Factories Rules, calculated by the Inspector of Factories, paid via treasury receipt, due annually before 31 December with a Form 2 renewal return — structurally confirms the FGD's "send someone every year" account, though exact rupee figures could not be found. A separate 2017 RTPS gazette sets a longer 90-day timeline specifically for renewal/amendment/transfer, distinct from the 65-day fresh-grant figure.

A genuine official SilpaSathi step sequence was partly retrieved (portal visit → apply online → login/register → accept declaration → complete registration form) — more granular than the ED's zero-step account, though the manual's further sections (documents, fee payment, status tracking, certificate download) could not be fully retrieved.

Resolving even minor deficiencies requires manual resubmission, with no streamlined digital correction flow. Applicants must physically visit the office repeatedly to find out status.
fgd.timeline: One specific case cited: the applicant waited 3-4 months, and the process only moved once the departmental officer personally contacted them to request the required documents. Licence validity is only 1 year, requiring frequent re-engagement for renewal.
fgd.automation: Applications being online is an acknowledged improvement over the earlier manual process, but there is no real-time status tracking, no published SOP/process-flow, no automated deficiency notifications, and officials are hard to reach for clarification. Participants "have to visit the department office regularly to track the verification process."
fgd.documentsNote: No specific duplicate-document list given, but repeated resubmission is triggered whenever "deficiencies" or "minor discrepancies" are found at scrutiny.
fgd.deemed: Not mentioned at all by participants — notably, unlike UP/DNH&DD/AP, no deemed-approval day-count or mechanism was raised, consistent with the broader complaint that there is no institutionalised timeline/communication mechanism governing the process at all.
costs: Implied, not quantified

No specific INR figures were quantified in this FGD — unusual relative to the other states. The recurring annual compliance effort ("we have to send someone only to maintain compliance, every year") implies a standing time/intermediary cost; the 3-4 month wait implies an unmonetised delay cost.
complaints: Institutionalise a communication mechanism (SMS/email/portal) for status and deficiency updates.
Enhance the portal — checklists, real-time tracking, automated notifications.
Extend licence validity, or move to a permanent licence with an annual fee — explicitly modelled on how "Trade Licence has become much simpler with automatic renewal after payment."
Set up dedicated help desks/nodal officers; notify deficiencies immediately.
Introduce self-certification for small units instead of extensive inspection.
Wider publicity/awareness of the process itself.
contradictions: The official framing of an "online, digitally governed" licensing system is directly contradicted — participants say the digital system provides no real tracking or proactive communication, forcing physical office visits and reliance on being personally contacted by an officer (a 3-4 month real-world wait in the cited case).
The complete absence of any deemed-approval discussion is itself notable: businesses here appear unaware of, or unaffected by, any such safeguard.

SERVICE.name: Factory License
SERVICE.definition: A statutory license required under the Factories Act, 1948 (and corresponding State Factory Rules) to operate a factory employing workers with the aid of power, permitting manufacturing operations subject to occupational safety, health and welfare compliance.

COST_TYPES.d: Time spent by employees on activities to prepare for the application — filling the form, preparing documents, obtaining approvals/certificates from other departments. Captured as respondent-reported time only, across four sub-stages: understanding requirements, collecting/preparing documents, filling/submitting the application, and follow-ups/query response.

Additional investment a business must make to comply with mandatory technical, safety, environmental or infrastructure requirements — equipment purchases, structural modifications, mandatory testing, record-keeping. Only mandatory, regulation-driven spend counts; voluntary upgrades (e.g. a firm's own ISO certification) are excluded.
Fees paid to external professionals — architects, structural engineers, MEP consultants, legal/liaison agents — engaged to help obtain the approval or fulfil compliance.

The additional financial burden from delay beyond the prescribed timeline — idle labour cost, bank interest on a project loan, machinery depreciation/rental, and rent or lease cost during the idle period.

Fees payable directly to Government — application/form fee, scrutiny fee, development charges, labour cess, licence fee. Per CoR 2.0 methodology this is reported as-is from the department's own fee schedule, and is explicitly excluded from inter-State comparison — unlike the other four cost types, it is not used for benchmarking or ranking States.

KPIS.d: The number and sequence of discrete actions an applicant must complete, end to end, exactly as described by the official Expert Discussion — not a QCI-invented summary.
The prescribed/statutory processing time as stated by the official, where given. Several States did not state a numeric timeline at all — shown as a data gap rather than assumed.

Whether application, scrutiny, fee payment and status tracking happen online, and whether any physical department visit is still required of the applicant — distinct from a physical site inspection, which is a safety step present almost everywhere and is shown separately, not penalised.
The document checklist required, and whether officials or applicants flagged any of it as duplicated or redundant.
Whether the law treats the approval as automatically granted if the department does not act within the prescribed time, and after how many days.
